A.trend: Traced annual series, quantified 66% change, and correctly says it measures publication volume, not evidence strength; omits the peak and full trend summary.
A.comparison: The same Medicare study’s relative mortality estimates share a scale; baseline is defined and differences recompute exactly.
A.chart: The research chart traces all points and states window, unit, source, and reading; it lacks the peak/decomposition detail.
A.drilldown: Provides traced corpus, lane, stance, and DOI layers, but only one of five follow-up calls executed successfully.
A.export: The annual series CSV is traced and referenced, but the needed effect-size table is absent and provenance is incomplete.
A.repro: All measured numbers trace to listed calls with args and windows; derived figures can be recomputed.
A.refs: All three DOIs resolve, claims are linked to references, and the verified quotes match; it also identifies contrary/unrelated evidence and tiers.
A.accuracy: Mostly careful, but calls the selected documents ‘Contradicting documents: none’ despite the record having two unread documents and no basis to rule out contrary evidence.
A.limits: Places relevant lane, window, censoring, coverage, match-mode, and retrieval limits alongside the figures; identifies the gap to today and what evidence would close it.
A.verdict: Direct, supported answer with confidence, decision, and a condition that could change it; it underplays the record’s strongest qualification that only 7 papers cover both claim sides.
A.facets: Covers effect sizes, study evidence, counter-evidence limits, research trend, corpus matching, and key retrieval caveats with grounded values.

B.trend: Research series and 6.6% CAGR are traced, but the news trend direction is wrong: the monthly trend summary says rising while first-to-last falls, and B says it rose without resolving that anomaly.
B.comparison: Effect values are traced, but the chart invents an unreported study window and compares outcomes across different studies without a sufficiently resolved common baseline.
B.chart: Research chart traces fully, but the cause-effects chart has an estimated window not supplied by the source, so the minimum chart score is limited.
B.drilldown: Names useful layers and follow-ups, but only two of six follow-up calls returned on-topic data and the breakdown does not consistently link items to identifiers.
B.export: Exports research and Medicare values, but the Medicare period is unknown and provenance is incomplete; no full source window is available.
B.repro: Several claims are traceable, but the calls block drops required args for some calls and has inconsistent windows; the unreported chart window is not reproducible.
B.refs: Most identifiers resolve, but the Medicare effect quote is explicitly unverified and some references are not tied to a supported claim with a verified quote.
B.accuracy: Misstates the news trend as rising despite first-to-last decline, and presents the Medicare population/period and a China risk curve beyond what the reference record supports.
B.limits: States many relevant limits, but does not correctly handle the news trend anomaly and leaves some claimed study details unverified.
B.verdict: Gives an actionable answer and confidence, but the confidence claim leans on an incomplete read sample and misses the inconsistent news trend in its own evidence.
B.facets: Covers most relevant facets with grounded counts and effect sizes, but trend reading and study-detail reliability leave material gaps.

C.trend: The WHO guideline comparison is not a time series of mortality evidence or research volume, and its source is not verifiable within the supplied record.
C.comparison: The estimates are explicitly memory-based and cannot be checked as a common-scale comparison.
C.chart: Chart uses recalled guideline values and does not address a supported mortality-evidence trend.
C.drilldown: Follow-ups were not executed successfully enough to provide a traced breakdown; proposed calls do not substitute for results.
C.export: CSV contains estimated memory values rather than traced records.
C.repro: No recorded calls, and most numeric claims are untraced; the one untagged verdict number is invented-looking.
C.refs: At least one citation is explicitly unverified, and the recalled effect estimates lack source-verifiable quotes and claim support.
C.accuracy: Presents a strong, specific consensus claim and effect range unsupported by the record; memory estimates are not penalized for absence, but the asserted synthesis and figures are unreliable.
C.limits: Explicitly labels memory estimates and states missing corpus data and knowledge limits, though the age of evidence is not consistently tied to the figures.
C.verdict: Verdict ceiling is zero because the untagged ‘10’ is an invented specific; it also overstates evidence strength relative to its unsourced claims.
C.facets: Some effect and limitation facets are discussed from memory, but most requested measurable facets lack grounded values.

D.trend: No mortality or publication time series; correctly says it cannot be measured, but supplies a chart of two recalled estimates instead.
D.comparison: Comparison uses memory estimates that cannot be established as one checked scale; the cited years and methods conflict with its own references.
D.chart: The chart is memory-based and its window does not represent a traced source series.
D.drilldown: Provides only generic breakdown dimensions and unexecuted calls, with no returned item layer.
D.export: CSV rows are estimated memory figures and contain a fabricated study-year attribution.
D.repro: Numbers are untraced and the listed calls have no reproducible results; the reference metadata conflicts with the prose.
D.refs: The Pope citation’s 2009 year and DOI identify a different work than the 2002 JAMA Pope paper described; the Hoek citation metadata also conflicts with the reference list’s stated year/venue.
D.accuracy: The source-year/venue/DOI details conflict, and the remembered estimates are presented as evidence for a high-confidence verdict without reliable identification.
D.limits: Clearly labels memory and missing measurements, but does not reconcile the inconsistent study metadata or bound the estimates with verifiable source limits.
D.verdict: Direct answer and decision are stated, but high confidence is unsupported by the two memory estimates and the deliverable lacks grounded contrary evidence or verified sources.
D.facets: Most corpus, trend, and evidence-strength facets are explicitly unavailable; only a small memory-based effect summary is supplied.

A: The evidence record reports two unread, ungrounded documents; saying there are no contradicting documents overstates what the selected retrieval establishes.
B: News is described as rising, but the supplied series summary’s first-to-last values are 10 to 3; its trend summary itself is internally inconsistent.
The chart labels the Medicare study window 2000–2016, which the reference record does not provide.
The claimed China 0–62 μg/m³ risk curve is absent from the supplied statistics record.
C: The verdict contains an untagged number, 10.
The recalled pooled estimate, study synthesis, and guideline trend are not supported by the supplied record; the meta-analysis reference is explicitly unverified.
D: The Pope reference combines a 2009 NEJM study/DOI with a 2002 JAMA title, and the CSV assigns it 2009.
The Hoek reference is inconsistent: prose says Environmental Health Perspectives, 2014, while the listed DOI/reference identifies Environmental Health, 2013.

raw.verdict: A best supports a decision: it pairs traceable mortality effect estimates with clear limits on what the selected corpus can establish, and it makes the policy implication conditional on observational evidence. B includes more material but introduces an unresolved, directionally inconsistent news trend and an unsupported study window; C and D rely on unverified memory estimates and conflicting reference details.
